Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Importance.

Heart-rate variability (HRV) is studied extensively as a prognostic marker in critical illness, yet the electrocardiographic sampling rate at which HRV is computed systematically distorts the resulting values.
Whether the associations between HRV and clinical outcomes reported in the literature are partly a consequence of this distortion has not been examined directly.
NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
Setting and data sources.

Two critical-care waveform databases with different native sampling rates (MIMIC-IV Waveform, approximately 250 Hz; MIMIC-III Waveform Matched p04, 125 Hz) and an independent 500-Hz reference cohort (PTB-XL) for mechanism validation.
The outcome association was estimated in 1,445 ICU stays from MIMIC-III p04, of whom 141 died in hospital (9.8%).
Native ECG sampling rate as a negative-control exposure; SDNN, RMSSD and heart rate as the measured exposures whose associations with mortality are evaluated.
Main outcomes and measures.
In-hospital mortality.
Distortion coefficients were obtained by end-to-end reprocessing of 7,293 original waveform segments with a fixed QRS detector.
Corrected odds ratios were reported as QBA sensitivity bands rather than point-identified effects.
Misclassification was quantified as the proportion of recordings below a 20 ms HRV threshold reclassified above it by coarse sampling.
Results.

End-to-end reprocessing gave an RMSSD distortion coefficient of 1.1575 (95% CI 1.0835-1.2492; 2,276 segments in 188 patients) for 250→62.5 Hz and 1.0588 (95% CI 1.0294-1.1033; 4,988 segments) for 125→62.5 Hz; high-frequency power was more affected than low-frequency power (1.2033 vs 1.0716).
Under the multiplicative model, an observed crude RMSSD-mortality odds ratio of 1.802 corresponded to a corrected interval of 1.8335-1.915 across the coefficient's 95% CI.
The correction was small relative to confounding: the same association fell to 1.116 after age adjustment.
Coarse sampling reclassified 33.70% of low-HRV recordings in MIMIC-IV and 20.72% in MIMIC-III, a larger potential source of bias than the continuous-scale correction.

The cross-database negative-control gradient was completed after linking both waveform cohorts to hospital outcomes: RMSSD inflation was reproducible (median ×1.101 at 125→62.5 Hz in MIMIC-III and ×1.270 at 250→62.5 Hz in MIMIC-IV), but the ageadjusted HRV-mortality risk ratio did not increase at lower rates (MIMIC-III 1.70→1.21; MIMIC-IV 1.31→1.29→1.20; all 95% CIs crossed 1).
The falsification test was therefore negative in these cohorts, and we report it as such rather than as evidence that measurement bias is absent.
Sampling rate is a detectable and correctable source of bias in HRV-outcome research.

Recording the sampling rate of each signal, stratifying effects by baseline variability, and reporting a QBA sensitivity band before dichotomising HRV would make published associations more interpretable.
The object of inference here is the measurement-error method, not a new clinical biomarker; the proposed reporting steps require no additional data collection.

To evaluate whether between-database differences in native ECG sampling rate can be used as a negative-control exposure to detect measurement-driven bias in HRV-outcome associations, and to quantify the sensitivity of a published association to an empirically measured distortion coefficient using quantitative bias analysis (QBA).
A methods investigation in three parts.
Part I sets out the causal structure and states why a strict instrumental-variable (IV) design is inappropriate here.
Part II derives a bias-correction factor under a multiplicative measurement-error model and propagates the empirical confidence interval of the distortion coefficient as a sensitivity band.
Part III applies the procedure to an observed HRV-mortality association from a single ICU waveform database, and examines the separate bias arising from threshold-based categorisation.
Reduced heart-rate variability (HRV) is one of the most widely reported physiological correlates of critical illness.

Reviews in critical care describe inverse associations between HRV and severity or mortality across diagnostic groups [6, 9, 10], and cohort studies have reported that changes in HRV precede the clinical recognition of sepsis [7, 8].

text.text: These findings have encouraged proposals that HRV might serve as a prognostic biomarker at the bedside [6].

text.text: The literature is also heterogeneous.

Sampling protocols, segment lengths, QRS detectors and frequency-band definitions differ substantially between studies, and reviews have noted that part of the apparent HRV-mortality association tracks heart rate rather than autonomic variability [9, 10].

Hejjel and Roth, using model tachograms, showed that time-domain error rises steeply as the sampling interval widens: at a 10 ms interval, the relative accuracy error for SDNN exceeded 30% in low-variability series [2].

text.text: The magnitude of the distortion also depends on how downsampling is performed: a recent preprint showed that extremapreserving schemes retain QRS-detection accuracy and RMSSD down to 12 Hz in the MIT-BIH databases, whereas naïve decimation fails below 45 Hz [43].

text.text: Our reanalysis uses straight decimation, as in the original pipeline, so the coefficients reported here describe that specific processing choice rather than sampling rate alone.
What these studies share is a focus on measurement accuracy.
They stop at the question of how far a computed HRV value departs from its true value.
The two literatures have not been brought together.

Although reviewers of critical-care HRV have noted sampling-rate heterogeneity as a source of between-study inconsistency [8, 10], we are aware of no study that treats the between-database difference in native sampling rate as a diagnostic instrument for bias in an HRVoutcome association, or that uses a measured distortion coefficient to correct such an association.

text.text: Here we make three claims.

First, sampling rate can be used as a negative-control exposure in the sense used by Lipsitch and colleagues and elaborated by Arnold and colleagues: a variable that should not be related to the outcome through the biological pathway of interest, but that shares the measurement and selection processes capable of generating a spurious association [20, 21].
text.formatted: First, sampling rate can be used as a negative-control exposure in the sense used by Lipsitch and colleagues and elaborated by Arnold and colleagues: a variable that should not be related to the outcome through the biological pathway of interest, but that shares the measurement and selection processes capable of generating a spurious association <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref>.

text.text: Second, because the distortion coefficient can be estimated directly from original waveforms, the magnitude of the resulting bias can be propagated formally rather than merely acknowledged, following the logic of quantitative bias analysis [11, 13, 14, 18].
text.formatted: Second, because the distortion coefficient can be estimated directly from original waveforms, the magnitude of the resulting bias can be propagated formally rather than merely acknowledged, following the logic of quantitative bias analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18]</ref>.

text.text: Third, the categorisation of HRV at a fixed threshold introduces a distinct misclassification problem that may dominate the continuous-scale correction.
We also state one claim we do not make.
We do not propose sampling rate as a valid instrumental variable.
Recording rate is correlated with centre, device era and monitoring intensity, so both independence from confounders and the exclusion restriction fail.
We therefore do not attempt causal identification.

The design is a bias audit: we ask how sensitive an observed association is to a measured measurement-error process, and we report a sensitivity band rather than a corrected point estimate with a claim of validity.
The manuscript is organised in three parts.
Part I defines the causal structure and the negative-control logic.
Part II derives the correction factor and specifies how the distortion coefficient is propagated.
Part III applies the procedure to a real outcome association and examines threshold misclassification.

The same distortion coefficients are used throughout, and they were estimated from the waveforms before any outcome association was considered; this separation is the methodological discipline of the design.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: Let S denote the native sampling rate of the ECG used to derive an RR-interval series, H* the underlying physiological HRV signal, Hobs the value computed from the digitised signal, C a set of common causes (age, illness severity, centre, device era, monitoring intensity, mean heart rate), and Y the clinical outcome.

Sampling rate affects the observed value through R-peak time quantisation, S → Hobs → Y; the physiological signal enters the observation through H* → Hobs; and the common causes influence S, Hobs and Y.

The negative-control premise is that S has no pathway to Y other than through the measurement of H* and through its association with C. If the Hobs-Y association is entirely physiological, conditioning on C should remove any dependence on S. An association that persists, and whose gradient across sampling-rate tiers matches the direction and magnitude of the independently measured distortion coefficients, is evidence that measurement artifact contributes to the estimate.

Negative controls of this form are best understood as a falsification test, not as a proof: as Arnold and colleagues emphasise, they can indicate the presence of bias without determining its direction or magnitude [21], and a null result cannot establish that bias is absent [20, 22]; methods that exploit negative controls for partial identification, such as the control-outcome calibration approach [23], require assumptions we are not in a position to make here.
text.formatted: Negative controls of this form are best understood as a falsification test, not as a proof: as Arnold and colleagues emphasise, they can indicate the presence of bias without determining its direction or magnitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>, and a null result cannot establish that bias is absent <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>; methods that exploit negative controls for partial identification, such as the control-outcome calibration approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>, require assumptions we are not in a position to make here.

text.text: The choice rules out a strict IV analysis.

For S to be a valid instrument it would need to be independent of C, which is contradicted by the clustering of recording equipment within centres and device generations, and it would need to affect Y only through the measured HRV, which is contradicted by the fact that sampling rate is a marker of the surrounding monitoring environment.

Causal diagrams for measurement bias [28, 29] and for monitoring-driven confounding in intensive care [30] make the same point from different directions: the monitoring process is itself related to patient state.

text.text: We therefore use S only as a bias scale, and we interpret the resulting estimates as sensitivity analyses in the sense of Greenland and of Lash and colleagues [11, 14].

text.text: The distortion coefficients were estimated by end-to-end reprocessing of original waveforms, using the same detection and HRV pipeline at each sampling rate.
A fixed QRS detector (wfdb gqrs) was applied to 7,293 segments: 2,294 from MIMIC-IV at native 250 Hz and 4,999 from MIMIC-III p04 at native 125 Hz.
Segments were then downsampled in stages to 62.5 Hz, and HRV indices were recomputed from the detected beat times at each stage.
All HRV values used in this analysis were recomputed in this way; none were read from the intermediate tables used for the earlier submission.

text.text: Suppose the measured exposure is a multiplicative distortion of the physiological one, Hobs = δ H*.
Under a logistic model in the true exposure, logit Pr(Y) = β + β H*, fitting against Hobs yields a slope of approximately β/δ when the error is non-differential and the model is correctly specified.
On the odds-ratio scale this gives OR_true = OR_obs ^ δ.

The derivation assumes a constant multiplicative factor over the exposure range; in practice δ varies with baseline variability and frequency band, so the result should be read as a first-order approximation.
The direction of the adjustment is worth stating explicitly.

Because δ > 1 inflates the exposure scale, the slope estimated against the inflated values is compressed towards the null; the correction therefore moves the odds ratio away from 1 on the multiplicative scale.
text.formatted: Because δ > 1 inflates the exposure scale, the slope estimated against the inflated values is compressed towards the null; the correction therefore moves the odds ratio away from 1 on the multiplicative scale.

text.text: That the correction increases an already positive odds ratio is not evidence that the association is an artifact; it is a consequence of the error model, and it is why the size of the correction must be compared with the size of the association and with changes under confounding adjustment.
Following the good-practice recommendations for QBA [12, 13], we treat δ as a bias parameter with an empirical distribution rather than a fixed constant.

text.text: The 95% confidence interval of the measured coefficient is used as the sensitivity band, giving OR_true(δ_lo) to OR_true(δ_hi).
This is a sensitivity analysis, not probabilistic bias analysis: we do not assign a probability distribution to δ, and we do not report a single "corrected" estimate as if it were identified.
No external validation data were needed because the bias parameter came from the end-to-end waveform reprocessing described above [11, 18].

Heart rate is retained as a negative control exposure in the strict sense: its measurement depends on R-R interval counting and should not be distorted by the sampling rates considered here, so δ = 1 and no correction is applied.
If sampling rate were generating associations indiscriminately, the heart-rate association would move as well; it does not.
Separate from the continuous-scale correction, we examined the effect of coarse sampling on a common reporting practice: classifying HRV as low when it falls below a 20 ms threshold.
Using the reprocessed waveforms, we computed the proportion of recordings below the threshold at the reference rate that were moved above it by downsampling.

This is an outcome-independent misclassification of the exposure, and its consequences for an odds ratio depend on the prevalence of low HRV and on the true association; we therefore report the reclassification fractions as the primary quantity and treat their effect on association estimates as a sensitivity consideration rather than a precise correction [18, 38, 39, 40].

We do not construct a negative-control outcome, because a candidate would need to share the confounders of HRV without lying on the autonomic pathway to mortality; none could be constructed credibly from the available tables, and inventing one would defeat the purpose of the test [20, 21].

Our approach is complementary to recent work that combines negative controls with empirical calibration to attribute a share of an observed association to systematic bias [19, 26, 27].

text.text: For the crude RMSSD-mortality association (OR_obs = 1.802), QBA gave OR_true = 1.8655 at δ = 1.0588, with a sensitivity band of 1.8335-1.915 over δ = 1.0294-1.1033.
For SDNN the corresponding interval was 1.4181-1.4541 around a point estimate of 1.4323, using the borrowed timedomain coefficient.
After age adjustment, the RMSSD association was 1.116 and the corrected interval was 1.1196-1.1287; under the stricter g-computation adjustment it was 1.154, corrected to 1.1589-1.1712.
Heart rate was unchanged at 1.350, 1.609 and 1.451 in the three models.
The multiplicative correction scaled with the magnitude of the observed association: the proportional shift was about 3.5% at the crude RMSSD estimate and under 1% at the age-adjusted estimate.
In other words, the measurement correction is largest where the crude association is largest, and it becomes negligible once the association has been reduced by confounding adjustment.
This ordering matters for interpretation: in these data, adjustment for measured confounders changed the estimate far more than the sampling-rate correction did.
Coarse sampling moved 33.70% of MIMIC-IV recordings initially below 20 ms above the threshold (182 of 540 segments), and 20.72% of MIMIC-III recordings (246 of 1,187).

Because a threshold defines the exposed group in many published HRV studies, this form of bias is not equivalent to the continuous-scale correction and can be larger in its effect on a reported odds ratio.
Reporting the sampling rate of every signal is therefore a prerequisite for comparing studies that use the same nominal threshold.

The direction required by the negative-control test is available from the distortion coefficients: lower sampling rates and lower baseline variability produce larger inflation, and HF is affected more than LF.
Having linked both waveform cohorts to hospital outcomes, we estimated the outcome association within each sampling-rate tier.

End-toend segments were restricted to durations of at least 60 s, aggregated to the median RMSSD per subject per tier, and split at the tertiles; the age-adjusted risk ratio for high versus low variability was obtained by marginal standardisation from a logistic model, with 95% confidence intervals from 1,500 subject-level bootstrap resamples.

The measurement gradient was reproducible -median RMSSD rose by ×1.101 from 125 to 62.5 Hz in MIMIC-III and by ×1.270 from 250 to 62.5 Hz in MIMIC-IV -but the association gradient was not: the risk ratio fell from 1.70 to 1.21 in MIMIC-III and from 1.31 to 1.20 in MIMIC-IV, and every interval crossed unity (Table 3, Figure 2).

text.text: We report this as a negative falsification test, not as evidence that measurement bias is absent.
We asked whether a known measurement artifact could account for part of the HRVoutcome associations that appear in the critical-care literature.

Using sampling rate as a negative-control exposure and a measured distortion coefficient as a bias parameter, we found that the correction to a crude RMSSD-mortality odds ratio was small (1.802 to an interval of 1.8335-1.915), that it shrank to under 1% after confounder adjustment, and that threshold-based classification was a more substantial source of potential bias, moving around one fifth to one third of low-HRV recordings across the threshold.
The results do not show that published HRV associations are artifacts.
They show that the artifact has a measurable, bounded effect, and that the effect can be reported rather than ignored.
The negative-control framing is useful precisely because it separates two hypotheses.
A genuinely physiological HRV-outcome association should not depend on the recording equipment's sampling rate.
An association that strengthens at lower rates, and by an amount compatible with δ, would implicate measurement.
With the outcome linkage now in place, the falsification test could be run in full.

It returned a negative result: although the measurement inflation was reproducible, the HRV-mortality association did not strengthen at lower sampling rates in either cohort, and none of the tier-specific risk ratios excluded unity.
Read as a falsification test, this does not confirm a measurement-driven association; nor, with 10 and 35 deaths in the two cohorts, does it exclude one.

The defensible reading is that the sampling-rate gradient is not a sensitive diagnostic at the sample sizes available here, which is precisely why the QBA sensitivity band -rather than the gradient -carries the quantitative argument.
Several features of the design merit emphasis.
The bias parameter was estimated from original waveforms rather than assumed, which is the condition under which QBA is most informative [11, 18, 19].

text.text: Negative-control and QBA approaches were used as diagnostics and sensitivity tools rather than as instruments for identification [20] [21] [22] [23].

text.text: Heart rate, which should be rate-invariant under the detection method, was carried through every model as a control exposure and remained unchanged.
And the two bias mechanisms -continuous inflation and threshold misclassification -were quantified separately, because a single correction would obscure the larger of the two.
The limitations are substantial.

Sampling rate is collinear with centre and device generation in these databases, so the negative-control exposure is not independent of the care environment; this is the reason for avoiding an IV interpretation and for presenting a sensitivity band rather than a causal effect.
The benchmark HRV-outcome association used for the QBA comes from one database at one native rate.

The crossdatabase gradient that we were able to run is underpowered: the linked waveform subsets contained 97 subjects with 10 deaths in MIMIC-III and 163 subjects with 35 deaths in MIMIC-IV, and the tier-specific confidence intervals were wide and all crossed unity.

Sampling rate is also strongly confounded with centre and device generation in these databases, and the sampling-rate tiers within a cohort arise from reprocessing the same recordings rather than from independent devices, so the gradient is a withinrecording sensitivity analysis and not a between-device comparison.

The exposure units of the source odds ratios are not documented in enough detail in the source report to make the correction more precise than a first-order approximation, and the SDNN coefficient is borrowed from RMSSD.
PTB-XL segments are ten seconds long and cannot support LF/HF analysis, so frequency-domain validation rests on the ICU waveforms alone.
Finally, the source association is counter-intuitive in direction and attenuates sharply with age adjustment; we use it as a test case for the method, not as evidence for a clinical claim.
These constraints point to a modest reporting recommendation rather than a new analytical standard.

Studies reporting HRV-outcome associations could state the sampling rate of each signal, report effects stratified by baseline variability where sample size allows, name the QRS detector and interpolation method, and show a QBA sensitivity band before presenting a dichotomised HRV analysis.
Each step uses information already available to the analyst.

The goal is not to establish a universal sampling-rate threshold -the appropriate rate depends on the HRV index and the variability range, as Zhou and colleagues and Burma and colleagues show [1, 3] -but to make the influence of the chosen rate visible.
text.formatted: The goal is not to establish a universal sampling-rate threshold -the appropriate rate depends on the HRV index and the variability range, as Zhou and colleagues and Burma and colleagues show <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref> -but to make the influence of the chosen rate visible.

text.text: Differences in ECG sampling rate are a measurable source of bias in HRV-outcome research.

Using sampling rate as a negative-control exposure and an empirically estimated distortion coefficient, we found a bounded effect on a continuous association and a larger effect on threshold-based classification.
The method is a bias audit, not a causal design and not a clinical test.
Reporting sampling rate, baseline-stratified effects and a quantitative sensitivity analysis would allow readers to judge how much of an HRV association survives the measurement process.
